blocks.prompt: The Green Top Full of Buds
blocks.text: Broccoli grows on a farm or in a garden. It likes cool weather best. Broccoli grows on a thick green stalk. The bumpy green top is called a crown. Those tiny green bumps are really flower buds. If a farmer does not pick the broccoli, the buds open up. They turn into small yellow flowers. We pick broccoli before that happens, while the buds are still closed and green. Then we can cook it or eat it raw. Broccoli is full of good things that help your body stay well.

blocks.prompt: How Farmers Made Broccoli
blocks.text: Broccoli belongs to the cabbage family. Its cousins are cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts. Long ago there were no broccoli plants at all. Farmers in Italy made broccoli by choosing wild cabbage plants with the biggest flower buds and planting their seeds, year after year, for a very long time. Slowly the plants changed. The buds grew larger and closer together, until they formed the thick green heads we know today. The green part you eat is a bundle of tiny flower buds. If the plant is left alone, those buds bloom into little yellow flowers, and the broccoli goes soft and bitter. So farmers pick it while the buds are still tight and green. Broccoli likes cool weather. It grows well in spring and fall. It is packed with vitamin C. In fact, weight for weight, broccoli holds more vitamin C than an orange.

blocks.prompt: The Vegetable That Never Grew Wild
blocks.text: Broccoli did not exist in the wild. There is no place on Earth where you can walk into a field and find it growing on its own. Broccoli is something people built, slowly, out of a scruffy seaside plant called wild cabbage. Wild cabbage still grows along the coasts of Europe. It is a loose, leafy plant with a bitter taste. Thousands of years ago, farmers noticed that some of these plants grew fatter clusters of flower buds than others. They saved seeds from those plants and grew them again. Each generation, they kept the plants with the biggest, tightest buds. This slow choosing is called selective breeding. Over many centuries in Italy, it turned a bitter weed into broccoli. The same wild cabbage was shaped in other directions too. Farmers who wanted big leaves bred kale. Farmers who wanted a fat bud at the top bred cabbage. Farmers who liked side buds bred Brussels sprouts. Broccoli, cauliflower, kale, cabbage, and Brussels sprouts are all the same species, just guided into different shapes by human choice. The part of broccoli we eat is a head of unopened flower buds sitting on a thick stalk. Picked young, the buds are sweet and green. Left on the plant, they burst into yellow flowers and the head turns bitter. Broccoli reached American plates in the 1920s, when Italian farmers began growing it in California and shipping it across the country.

blocks.prompt: A Garden of Flowers That Never Bloomed
blocks.text: Every head of broccoli is a garden of flowers that never got to bloom. The bright green surface, if you look closely, is made of thousands of tiny buds packed tightly together. Each one is a flower waiting to open. Farmers cut the broccoli while those buds are still shut, because a closed bud is tender and sweet, and an open one is stringy and bitter. If a plant is left in the ground too long, the head loosens, yellow flowers push out, and the vegetable is ruined for the table but perfect for making seeds. Broccoli has a strange history, because it has no wild ancestor of its own. It was invented. Its parent is wild cabbage, a tough, bitter plant that grows on the sea cliffs of Europe. Starting more than two thousand years ago, farmers in the Italian countryside began saving seeds only from the wild cabbage plants that grew the fattest flower buds. Season after season, the buds got larger and tighter, until they clustered into the green domes we now call broccoli. This method of choosing which plants get to reproduce is called selective breeding, and it is the same tool that turned wolves into dogs. The wild cabbage was patient raw material. Guided one way, it became broccoli. Guided another, the very same species became cabbage, kale, cauliflower, kohlrabi, and Brussels sprouts. That is why these vegetables can look so different yet share a family resemblance in taste and smell. Broccoli is not only clever history. It is also unusually good food. It carries plenty of fiber, which helps digestion, and it is loaded with vitamin C. Weighed gram for gram, broccoli actually holds more vitamin C than an orange. It thrives in cool weather and struggles in summer heat, which is why gardeners plant it in early spring or fall. Broccoli arrived in the United States fairly late. Italian immigrant farmers, including the D'Arrigo family in California, began growing it commercially in the 1920s and shipping it east by rail. Within a generation it went from unknown to ordinary.

blocks.prompt: The Vegetable People Invented
blocks.text: Walk through any grocery store and you will pass a vegetable with no home in the wild. Broccoli grows in fields and gardens all over the world, but there is nowhere on Earth you could hike into and discover it growing by itself. Unlike an apple tree or a blueberry bush, broccoli has no wild version. It is, in the most literal sense, a human invention, and its story reveals how much of what we eat was shaped by people rather than found in nature. The raw material was wild cabbage, known to botanists as Brassica oleracea. It is an unremarkable plant, loose-leafed and bitter, that still clings to the chalk cliffs along the coasts of Europe. More than two thousand years ago, farmers in the lands around the Mediterranean began to notice small differences between individual plants. Some grew fatter clusters of flower buds than others. Those farmers saved seeds from the plants they liked best and sowed them the following season, and they repeated that choice, year after year, for centuries. The buds that they favored grew steadily larger and tighter, until they packed together into the dense green heads we now call broccoli. Biologists call this process selective breeding: humans, not the environment, decide which individuals get to reproduce. What makes wild cabbage remarkable is how many different vegetables came out of it. Guided toward large leaves, it became kale and collard greens. Guided toward a single swollen bud, it became the cabbage head. Guided toward a fat, starchy stem, it became kohlrabi. Guided toward clusters of side buds along the stalk, it became Brussels sprouts. Broccoli and cauliflower are the versions bred for their flower heads. All of these plants are the same species. A cabbage and a Brussels sprout could, in principle, be crossed, because underneath their strange shapes they are the same creature wearing different costumes that people designed. The part of broccoli we actually eat tells its own story. Each green head is a tight bundle of hundreds of unopened flower buds. Harvested young, those buds are sweet and tender. Left in the field, they finish what they were always trying to do: they open into small yellow flowers, the head falls apart, and the plant sets seed. A ruined head of broccoli, from the plant's point of view, is a successful one. Broccoli is also worth eating for reasons beyond its history. It is rich in fiber and vitamin C, holding, gram for gram, more vitamin C than an orange. It prefers cool weather, which is why it is planted in spring and fall rather than the heat of midsummer. And it came to American tables surprisingly recently. Italian immigrant farmers, most famously the D'Arrigo brothers in California, began growing broccoli commercially in the 1920s and shipping it east by rail. A vegetable that took twenty centuries to build became an everyday sight in a single lifetime.
